passage:
For two winters I worked the night switchboard at a hotel in Buffalo, eleven to seven, and I came to think of the shift as having four weathers.

Until about one the board is domestic. Guests want ice, or a second pillow, or to know whether the restaurant is really closed, and they ask in the voice people use with a stranger they expect to see at breakfast. I put these through to housekeeping and wrote nothing down.

From one to three the calls come from outside. Someone in another time zone wants room 412 and will not be told that the hotel does not wake guests without a reason; someone’s brother-in-law, drunk and affectionate, wants to sing. This is the only stretch of the night that requires a policy. The policy was mine, since the night manager slept from one thirty and considered the arrangement confidential.

From three to about five the board goes quiet in a way that is not restful. You are alone with the hum of the panel and the knowledge that the next light will not be about ice. In two winters I took four calls in that window that mattered: a chest pain, a woman locked out on a fire escape in February, a man who wanted the name of a hospital and would not say why, and one I still have no category for. The training for these consisted of a laminated card with the fire department’s number, which I never needed, and the switchboard’s own logic, which is that you keep the line open while you find someone.

After five it is staff. The bakery calls to be let in at the loading door, the first taxis want the doorman, a housekeeper phones in sick and you can hear her children behind her.

People ask what the job was like and I say the hours were bad, which is true and is not the answer. The answer is that a building has a pulse, and most people are awake for only one beat of it.

In the spring of 1903 the harbor commission of Alder Cove, a fishing port of nine hundred people, met to settle a question it had deferred for six years. Hollis Vane, the engineer the town had hired the previous autumn, laid his plan before the seven commissioners: to cut a second entrance through the sand spit at Low Point, so that vessels need not beat around the shoal in a southerly wind. His estimate was fourteen thousand dollars, more than Alder Cove had ever borrowed at one time. When the meeting opened, the standing motion was the merchant Amos Kerr's, to do the work in stages over ten years and borrow nothing. Two commissioners, Pell and Danforth, had said nothing at all.

What moved them was neither Vane's drawings nor his figures. A letter came from an Army engineer at the district office, undertaking to match, dollar for dollar, whatever Alder Cove itself spent on the cut. Fourteen thousand dollars had suddenly become seven, and Pell and Danforth voted with Vane that evening.

Kerr's answer was not that the work was useless. It was that the district office had given two other towns the same undertaking within his memory and had honored it in neither of them. He lost, five to two, and the town borrowed in June.

The town dug its own half of the cut in 1904 and stopped. The federal money arrived in 1912 and came to less than a third of the sum promised. The entrance was opened to nine feet and never to the fifteen Vane had drawn; vessels used it in fair weather and avoided it in foul. Whether it would have answered at full depth cannot be said. Vane left in 1908 for a larger post, and the minute book gives the whole business one line.

passage:
My grandmother was the last jobbing printer on Ferris Street, and her shop closed the winter I turned nine. My family repeats five reasons: her failing eyesight, a rent the landlord doubled, her partner Ines leaving for Dunmore, a copy shop across the street, and a flood in the cellar that spoiled the paper. Last spring I read her ledgers.

The ledgers settle it: the landlord doubled the rent. March's entry is twice February's, and she asks what a press would fetch. Her eyesight held; she read register marks by lamplight that winter. Ines stood at the stone until the final week. The copy shop opened the spring after the doors shut. The cellar stayed dry, and the paper went on unspoiled.

That last night she set the handbill on the stone, deposited among the rest. No type was arranged; the cases stayed shut under cloths. No day was appointed, and the carter came when he pleased. The ink never hardened, though she washed the slab at ten. The sun had not descended; the chimneys were still bright. The ledger's last page corrects a guess of mine: I had put the closing a year early. No date stands there to fix the order of anything. Her handwriting is not on it; a bindery clerk kept the book. It shows nothing of how the work was priced. It names no others who worked there, only herself.

She needed a lease at a fixed rent, and the landlord signed none. Someone to read her proofs aloud she never needed. The bench beside her held a second printer trained already. Work no copier could match kept arriving all that winter. Her storeroom stood above the water and her reams stayed dry.

My admiration for how she closed the shop carries one regret: she might have told us. Unreserved my admiration is not, whatever the ledgers show. Her silence draws no criticism from me; she owed us nothing. Detachment is beyond me; the shop was my own family's. Nor does her stubbornness amuse me.

passage:
Learning the Tide Chart

My uncle keeps the chart above the sink,
a page of numbers small as grains of rice,
and every morning, before the kettle,
he runs one finger down the column.

For a year I thought this was a habit
like touching the doorframe on the way out,
the sort of thing a man does because his father did,
and I did not ask.

Then a Tuesday in October he said, Come,
and we walked to the flats at a quarter past six
where the water had gone off somewhere else
and left the whole bay standing open -

long ribs of sand, a stranded orange buoy,
a boat sitting down in the mud like a cow,
the mussel beds black and shining
as a kept promise.

Two hours, he said. Then it comes back
across this ground, faster than a man walks.
I looked at the drying sand and did not believe him.
But I had seen the page: six forty-two,

and a number that meant how far,
and the small letter L beside it
that meant the sea would be low,
and then would not.

Now I check it too, before the kettle.
It is not that I am afraid of the water.
It is that someone wrote down, years ago,
exactly when the door would stand open,

and where I live, that is the nearest thing
to being told a secret
and being trusted with it.

The mayfly hatch on Lake Ferrin once darkened the village streetlights for a week each June, and it has not done so since 2011. Five causes have been proposed: perch stocked for anglers, a dam trapping the silt the nymphs burrow in, fertilizer running off the lakeside farms, a raised weir drowning the shallows, and water warmer than before. Three summers of survey work point one way.

The surveys point to the dam. The silt the nymphs burrow in has not passed it since 2009, and the bed below is bare gravel. The stocked perch eat no nymphs, their stomachs holding snails. No algae bloom has formed; the farms' runoff stays low. The weir was never raised; its boards sit as in 1950. The lake runs no warmer than it did, June for June.

A spring feeds the north bay, a source of cold water all summer. Nothing climbs in that season; the shallows stay cold. The gauge holds no coil, working by float and chain. No trout leap for flies here, the lake having none. The trouble has no single origin anyone has found. The club's catch book dates the last big hatch to June of 2010. No change in the fishing appears there after the stocking. No members are named in it, only weights and dates. The catch book records no weather of any kind. No boast about the fishing is preserved there.

Return depends on passing silt below the dam, which a sluice could manage. Taking the perch out would gain nothing; the nymphs are safe from them. A buffer strip along the farms would catch runoff that never comes. Lowering the weir boards would uncover shallows never drowned. Cooler summers would help nothing, the lake being cool enough.

The club's conduct puzzles me; it paid for the survey and then ignored it. The club's conduct earns no praise from me. Its conduct rouses no anger in me. No hope comes to me from the club's conduct. Indifference is not what the club's conduct meets from me.

For as long as the famine of that decade has been written about, it has been explained by the weather. Three dry summers in a row, a harvest that failed twice, and a district that lost perhaps a tenth of its people: the chain seems complete, and the chronicles composed soon afterward assert it in almost those words.

The ledgers of the district’s grain houses, catalogued for the first time only recently, do not fit the chain. They show that the stores were not empty. In the worst of the three years the granaries of the market town held enough to feed the district for eleven weeks, and in those same twelve months the town shipped a little over a third of its stock downriver, where prices were higher. Grain left a starving district in daylight, under the seal of the magistrate who was also writing to the capital to ask for relief.

Historians who have read the ledgers divide over what they show. One group reads a failure of authority. The magistrate could have closed the river and did not, and the chronicles that blame the weather were written by men with reason to prefer that explanation. A second group reads something less deliberate. Prices, they point out, had risen fourfold while a labourer’s wage had not moved; the grain did not leave because anyone decided to starve the district but because nobody in it could outbid a buyer downstream. Closing the river would have kept the grain in the district without putting it within reach of the people who needed it.

What the ledgers cannot settle is whether the second account explains the first. A magistrate who understood that his townspeople could not buy the grain may have judged a ban pointless rather than simply declined to impose one. The letters that would show what he believed have not survived, and until they do the argument rests on a record of quantities and prices that was never meant to record intentions.

Borrowing at the Fenn Street library doubled between 2016 and 2019, while every other branch in the borough lost readers. Five causes have been offered: the rerouted number nine bus; the closing of the Bourne Road branch; the longer evening hours; the ending of overdue fines; a new school reading requirement. The borough's own data settle it.

The school rule accounts for it: the rise is confined to readers of eleven to fourteen, and began the term the rule took effect. The daytime totals rose as fast, and evening borrowing was flat. The number nine has kept its old route for thirty years. Bourne Road is open still, and not one card came over. Fines are charged as they always were, and no debt was forgiven.

A figure crosses the window at closing, which is the caretaker on his round. No number is quoted here, and eleven thousand is nobody's total. Mrs Aidoo is unknown outside the branch and opens no doors. Staff reckon nothing by hand; a machine does the arithmetic. The report carries no diagram, and its pages hold only text.

A counter on the door has logged every entry since 2012. Its use is age: entries are tied to cards, so the eleven-to-fourteens are picked out. It keeps no clock, and its entries carry no hour. No postcode is attached to an entry, and no line appears. Bourne Road's entries are kept elsewhere and never added in. No account is matched to an entry, and debts stay invisible.

Another branch could repeat the rise only by having a school set reading for its pupils; nothing else on that list moved these figures. The borough has had three years to copy this and has not stirred. The staff have earned no particular praise, and I offer none. The branch was funded generously and wanted for nothing. The numbers are sound; I would not have them counted again. I do not leave the judging to others; my verdict is plain.

passage:
The song a male sparrow sings is not invented. He learns it, during a few weeks of his first summer, from the adults within earshot, and the result is a local dialect: two valleys an hour’s walk apart can hold populations whose songs a practised ear separates at once. Because the learning window closes and the song then holds steady for life, a dialect was long treated as a fixed label — useful to researchers precisely because it could not change.

A programme of translocation put that usefulness to the test. To rebuild a population lost to a fire, fifty-one adult males were caught in one valley and released in another forty kilometres away, whose dialect differed in the placement of a single trill. The birds were recorded weekly. Within one breeding season thirty-eight of the fifty-one were singing the trill in its new position. The remaining thirteen never altered a note.

The obvious reading is that the window does not close after all, and that an adult sparrow can learn. A second reading has proved harder to dismiss. Young males, it turns out, memorise far more song than they ever perform: recordings made in a bird’s first summer catch fragments of neighbouring dialects that drop out of the repertoire before the first breeding season and were assumed to have been discarded. If those fragments are stored rather than discarded, the translocated males were not learning in adulthood but retrieving something learned on schedule and never used. The thirteen holdouts would then be the birds that had never happened to hear the second dialect as juveniles.

Choosing between the two readings would require knowing what each bird heard in its first summer, and for a wild-caught adult that is unknowable. So the question is being run forward instead. Nestlings are being raised within earshot of one dialect only, and will be moved as adults. If they acquire the new trill, storage cannot account for it, and something in the standard description of the learning window will have to give way.

The mural on Rowan Street Station's west stair is called the last work of the painter Cecile Mabry. Five accounts of its making circulate: that Mabry painted it herself, that her apprentice Tomas Vane finished it, that three sign-painters worked from her drawing, that the rival Halloran of Preswick was paid for it, and that her brother Emile copied an earlier panel. The station's papers opened last year.

The papers put the brush in the sign-painters' hands. Three were hired from the goods yard, and her drawing issued to them. Mabry never mounted the scaffold, being at Ashe that winter. Vane drew no wages that winter, being at work in Leeds. Halloran of Preswick was paid nothing, and his ledger shows none. Emile signed nothing and appears only as a mourner.

The ground for doubting the old label is a supplier's letter, a reason nobody had. No undercoat lies beneath the paint; plaster took the colour. There is no soil behind that wall, which backs onto the ticket hall. Nothing there serves as a background; figures crowd the wall. Whoever painted it lacked training in drawing, as the hands show. The reopening photograph shows how the concourse was lit. The mural has taken no damage since, so the photograph shows none. The photograph is undated and fixes nothing about the work. No figure in that crowd can be identified. The crowd's reaction goes unrecorded; every face is turned away.

The next step is to look for the squared drawing copyists would have marked. The brushwork of her signed canvases settles nothing; she never touched it. Hunting the walls Vane painted later is idle. Halloran's letters at Preswick prove nothing about a wall he never saw. No earlier panel exists; the design was invented here.

The station's silence since then annoys me more than the finding. My agreement with it is not settled. No reluctance holds me back; I accept it. Curiosity is not what it leaves me. I have no sympathy for anyone it displaces.

The bell above the door had been broken since spring, so Mira learned to know the customers by their footsteps: the slow scuff of the newspaper man, the twins who arrived at a run and left at a run. She had worked the register at her grandmother's shop every Saturday since March, and had come to think of the drawer as hers — the worn ridge in the coin tray, the rubber band she kept around the twenties.

On the last Saturday in October she forgot her jacket and went back for it after closing. Through the window she saw her grandmother at the counter with the drawer open, counting. Mira stood in the cold and watched her finger travel down the column of the receipt tape, stop, and go back up. Then her grandmother took a small purse from her coat pocket, counted out four bills, and laid them in the drawer.

Mira did not go in. She walked to the bus stop with her jacket over her arm and the word for it arriving near the corner: checked. She was being checked. Every Saturday since March. All that talk about trusting her with the shop, and a woman in an empty room counting after her.

She said nothing for a week. Then, on a Tuesday, flattening boxes for the recycling, she found the tapes in a bundle and read them the way her grandmother had, down the column. The totals were short. Not by much — three dollars, eleven, six. On the days she had worked the register alone, they were short. On the days her grandmother had worked it, they were not.

She sat down on the step with the tapes in her lap. Her grandmother had not been counting to catch her. She had been counting to find out how much, and paying it in from her own purse, so the books would balance and Mira would never be told. A whole spring and summer of it. Mira thought about the rubber band around the twenties, how carefully she had put it there, and how little that had ever had to do with anything.

The ice on Miller's Pond goes out about two weeks earlier than it did when the town began writing the date down in the 1840s. A survey team spent four springs on the water asking why. Road dust does no work on the sheet: the team painted test panels on the ice, dusting half and sweeping half clean, and both sets melted through on the same day. The new dam sends no warmth down: loggers above and below the inflow agreed within a tenth of a degree all spring, and the years the gates stood shut changed nothing. Cores cut through snow and ice show the cover not changed at all, in March or in the weeks after ice-out, and the deepest-drifted bays open with the bare ice. The spring winds have not shifted: the ridge gauges give the same March run as the oldest charts, and the calmest springs broke up no later than the windiest.

The thermometer records are the whole of the case: a century of morning readings taken in one shelter on the ridge. March has warmed steadily across that century, and the warmest Marches in the column stand beside the earliest ice-outs, year for year. Warm air works on a sheet from above all month, and the pond now loses in March what it used to lose in April.

Two weeks of open water in March is two weeks more sun in the pond, and the trout spawn earlier for it. On the morning the sheet broke this spring, the dial in the shelter registered nine degrees above freezing before eight. Nothing in the four seasons caught us off guard, and every question we raised now has its answer. The same work would settle any pond of this size, and the town's questions were fair, a pleasure to answer. The case on this pond is closed, and nothing in it remains open.

passage: Arlen and Wyke sit nine miles apart on the same estuary, and for three centuries the difference between them was too small to interest anyone. Both had a tidal harbor, both sent out wool and barley and took in coal, and in 1850 they handled tonnages within a tenth of each other. In 1854 a branch line reached the estuary and, because the ground north of the river was firmer, ran to both towns. A railway at a port does not by itself move goods; it changes the place where goods are handed from one carrier to another, and the handing over is done by carts. Here the two towns differed, and the difference was old enough that nobody had thought of it as an economic policy. Arlen's carters had been a chartered company since 1611, and the charter reserved carriage within the town to men who had served a seven-year apprenticeship under a freeman of the company. Wyke had no such body; its carting had always been done by farmers in the slack season, and anyone with a horse could take a load. When the railway opened, a merchant in Wyke who wanted forty tons moved from a siding to a quay hired whoever was standing there. The same merchant in Arlen could hire only from a company of thirty-one men, whose number the charter fixed and whose rates it set. Within four years the estuary's transshipment trade had gathered at Wyke; by 1861 Wyke was handling three and a half times Arlen's tonnage, and the warehouses rising along the new sidings were rising there. Arlen's company saw the problem and petitioned to open its rolls in 1866, and the charter was amended in 1869. It made no difference. The warehouses, the bonded stores and the agents' offices were in Wyke by then, and they were not going to be moved nine miles because carting in Arlen had become cheaper. The comparison is useful precisely because the two towns are otherwise so alike; it is hard to find another case in which the want of a single rule is so nearly the only variable.

passage:
Ask why the tomato took so long to reach the British table and you will be told that people thought it poisonous. The story is on museum labels and in the front matter of cookbooks: the tomato belongs to the nightshade family, so for two centuries Britons grew it for ornament and would not eat it.

The explanation should be dropped altogether. The trouble is not that the evidence for it is thin; the trouble is that the evidence runs the other way. English herbals describe the plant from the 1590s, and those that mention eating it mention it calmly, as something done in Spain and Italy rather than as something fatal. Gardening manuals of the 1700s give instructions for raising the fruit for the kitchen. If a fear had been general, these writers are exactly the people who would have recorded it, and they did not.

What did hold the tomato back is duller and far better attested: the plant would not ripen. A tomato needs a long warm season, and the English summer supplies neither reliably. Growers got green fruit in most years, and green fruit, in a kitchen with no tradition of cooking it down, is simply not food. The nightshade story explains a refusal. There was no refusal to explain — only a crop that failed.

The dates settle the matter. Tomatoes entered ordinary British cookery not when a superstition lifted but when glass became cheap. Sheet glass and hot-water piping made the commercial glasshouse practical in the 1830s and 1840s, and tomato recipes appear in ordinary household books within that same generation: not a decade after any change in belief, but a decade after a change in horticulture.

The poison story survives because it is a better anecdote than a greenhouse. It supplies the past with a vivid error to be rescued from, which flatters the present, and it can be repeated without reading anything. The truer account asks for a little more: a seed catalogue, a weather record, and the price of glass.

Every few years somebody proposes to fix the long race. The suggestions vary - shorten it, break it into heats, show only the leaders - but the reasoning is always the same: nothing happens for most of an hour, and audiences will not sit still for it. The reasoning has a point buried in it, and I will come back to that point. It is wrong about what the event is.

A short race is a comparison of top speeds. You watch eight bodies do the same thing at once, the fastest wins, and it is thrilling, and it is over before you have chosen anybody to care about. A long race is a comparison of decisions. In the ninth lap a runner lying fourth works out that she has one surge and not two, and spends it, and you can see her decide. The runner who wins may have spent twenty minutes in fifth place doing arithmetic - how much is left, how much the leader has used, what the wind on the back straight will cost. None of that exists in a race that lasts ten seconds, and none of it can be manufactured by cutting to the leaders, because the leaders are precisely the part of the picture where the decisions have already been made.

Now the point I promised to come back to, which is a real one: the middle of a long race is genuinely hard to watch, and the sport has not helped itself. Commentary that names only the front three, and cameras that follow the same three, teach an audience that the rest is filler. A spectator who has never run has no way to know that the pace has quietly risen, or that a runner who drifts wide on a bend has lost more than a stride. That is a failure of coverage, not a failure of the event. Show the gap closing at the back. Put the lap times on screen where newcomers can read them.

Do that, and the hour stops being empty. Shorten the race instead, and you will have kept the audience by removing the reason to watch.

passage:
Hester Vane's 1834 chart of the Vole Reach stayed on the pilots' shelves seventy years, long after grander surveys were thrown out. Five reasons are offered for its authority: a flood that bared the bed; her three winters of soundings; the engraver's uncommonly fine hand; the backing of a merchant house; her refusal to sell the plates. Her own papers settle the question.

Her papers credit the soundings: she ran the same eighty lines each winter for three years and averaged them. The Trent house paid her nothing; she hired her own boats. She sold the plates in 1836, and copies circulated freely. No flood bared the bed in her lifetime, dry or otherwise. The engraving is coarse, and pilots complained of it for years.

Her lodging stood close to the staithe, three doors from the ferry steps. The workroom was never barred, and its door stood open nightly. The loft stayed airy in all weathers, with wind through it. She was open about her method and taught any pilot. Her count of the shoals was rough, never exact.

The ledger of her expenses survives in the borough archive. What the ledger supplies is a tally of winters: each season's boat hire is entered. No draft from any merchant house is entered anywhere in it. No offer for the plates appears in it, struck through or otherwise. The months of 1831 are missing from it, and no dates survive. Bewick's fee is nowhere in it, the cutting having been paid elsewhere.

Those three winters of soundings are what a rival would have had to equal; nothing else on that list gave the chart its authority. She was, without qualification, the finest riverman of her generation. She published everything she had, and I regret no silence. Nothing in her character puts me off; the reports are warm. I distrust nothing told of her, and check none of it. She was no ordinary surveyor, and I refuse to call her one.

passage:
Marta Sandoval spent thirty years compiling the first dictionary of the dialect of the high mountain province, working at a kitchen table between teaching posts. What happened to those finished pages is still argued about in the valleys she recorded. No volume of her own was ever bound, and she never paid a printer anything at all. The university library asked twice for the manuscript, and she had still not answered when the slips left for the capital; nothing reached the library. A newspaper offered to print one letter of the alphabet a month, and she refused to let the work appear in parts. A compiler in the capital borrowed her slips for a summer, and eleven thousand of her entries stand in his national dictionary under his name. A publisher across the border wanted a translation, but nothing of hers appeared abroad in any language.

One market day a week for nineteen years she stood among the stalls asking sellers what they called things, certain that people speak most truly while haggling over goods. She began each market day with the same question, the old name for a measure of oil, and set down whatever the first stall told her. A word went onto a card the first time a seller said it, without waiting for a second mouth. Parish books and wills she never opened, holding that a word owes nothing to having once been written down. The village teachers offered to have their classes write to her, and she refused: a child's page reaches the post already corrected. She kept no correspondents in other villages, saying that one market draws twelve villages to it, so postbags were waste.

Her name appears nowhere in his three volumes, not even among the thanks. It is no comedy, and hardly a waste, since the words did survive; her stubbornness is not the point, and impatience would be misplaced. The feeling the story leaves is indignation on her behalf, at a theft nobody has yet called one.

Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.

Everyone has a plan for the kitchen.
Raise the floor eight inches, says Ruth.
Tile, not board, says her husband,
and put the outlets up at chest height.

They are not wrong. The river will come
again, in seven years or eleven,
and the outlets at ankle height
are the reason we have no stove.

But I notice they begin at the rebuild.
They arrive at the door with a plan
the way you bring a casserole:
something warm to set down and leave.

What I want is slower than tile.
I want someone to stand in the doorway
and let me say what was in the room.
The table my father cut down

to fit the corner when we moved,
which was too short for six, and we used it
for twenty years for six.
The tin of buttons. The step stool

with my brother's name in nail polish.
Say them back to me. Do not tell me
buttons can be replaced, which is true,
which is the least useful true thing.

Ruth, I will raise the floor.
I will put the outlets where you say.
But not this week. This week
the room is still a room to me

and not a site. So stand here.
Look where the water stopped
on the door frame, that grey line,
and say: it came this high, and this

is what it took. Then we can measure.
Then bring me the tile.

passage: Sleep is easy to recognize in a dog and hard to define in anything else, which is why researchers rely less on the word than on a checklist. Four conditions are usually required: the animal becomes less responsive to the world; the state reverses quickly when something important happens; it recurs on a daily rhythm; and, if the animal is kept from it, it takes more of it afterward. The fourth condition, called rebound, does the real work, because it separates sleep from stillness, and a stone is unresponsive but a stone does not catch up. Beroe pallens, a comb jelly of the cold water off southern Chile, has no brain at all; its nerve cells are spread through its body in a diffuse net. Ivar Lindqvist's laboratory kept forty under constant dim light and filmed the cilia along their combs, which normally beat without pause. Every animal slowed its beating for about ninety minutes, at the same point in each twenty-four-hour cycle, and returned to full speed within seconds when dye was released in the water near it. Three of the four conditions were met cleanly. The crew then kept the animals from slowing, using a gentle current timed to the onset of each quiet period, for three cycles. The rebound they recorded was four minutes, a quiet period ninety-four minutes long instead of ninety, a difference so small that Lindqvist reports the figure without building anything on it. The checklist as written admits no exception, and by it B. pallens does not sleep. Lindqvist's response was not to argue for the animal but to question the fourth condition. Rebound, he points out, is a way of detecting a cost: an animal that must make up lost sleep has paid for going without. In a creature with no brain to restore, the cost may be smaller, and a condition built around mammals would then be measuring the size of that debt rather than its existence. He has proposed replacing rebound with any demonstrated cost of staying awake, such as slower healing or poorer capture of prey, and the committee that maintains the checklist has taken the question up.

passage:
For six summers Dr. Ines Varela's crew has climbed the same wet slope on Ketil Island before dawn, pushing a gloved arm into storm-petrel burrows to feel whether a chick is inside. The work is tedious and low-tech: a numbered stake at every burrow, a tally sheet in a plastic sleeve, and, by a rule Varela has never relaxed, a scale for every twentieth chick. Mainland colonies of the same bird have been shrinking for twenty years, so anything Ketil does differently is worth a season of somebody's life.

The tally sheets show occupied burrows on the seaward slope rising from 540 in the first season to 870 in the sixth, while the inland slope, walked the same way on the same mornings, ends where it began. The scale shows no difference between the two. Chicks weighed at twenty days old average the same on both slopes in every season of the study.

Varela credits the light rather than the food. In the study's third year the automated station on the headland traded its white lamp for a shielded red one, and the dawn walk changed with it: the grounded fledglings the crew once picked out of the gravel by the dozen, dazzled and unable to lift off again, now number two or three in a whole season. The seaward burrows are precisely the ones whose fledglings must pass beneath the lamp on their first flight out.

Ketil's introduced rats disappeared early in the study, and a visiting biologist has argued ever since that their removal is the whole story. Varela thinks that account fails on its own map: the traps were set in the inland turf, and the inland slope is the ground that gained nothing. Next summer she will visit three other stations that shielded their lamps.

Varela is careful about what a tally sheet can carry. "Six summers is six summers," she tells students who want a headline. "It is a pattern, not a law."
